title: Before you hunt: license, tags, orange, and this year's rules
context: Before a hunt you need a valid license and any tags for the animal, the hunter orange your state requires, and this season's official rules, which change every year. Also called hunting license, deer tag, what do I need to hunt, hunter orange, blaze orange. Look for license and tags on you, not at home; orange hat and vest where the state requires it.

title: Legal shooting light
context: Legal shooting light is the window each day when hunting is allowed; many states use about 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset, but the exact rule is set by each state and sometimes by species. Also called shooting hours, legal shooting time, half hour before sunrise, when can I shoot. Look for sunrise and sunset for your exact spot; the state's own rule for the species.

title: Firearm safety in the field
context: Field firearm safety comes down to four habits: treat every gun as loaded, keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot, and be sure of your target and what is beyond it. Also called gun safety, hunting gun safety, muzzle control, treat every gun as loaded, firearm rules. Look for muzzle never sweeps a person, including yourself; finger rests along the frame, outside the trigger guard.

title: Know your target and what is beyond it
context: Before any shot you must be certain of the species, sex if it matters for your tag, and that a safe backstop such as rising ground stops the bullet; anything uncertain means no shot. Also called identify before you shoot, not sure what it is, is it a deer, backstop, what is behind the target. Look for whole animal seen, not just a patch of brown or a sound; no house, road, trail, or person in the line of fire.

title: Shot placement and what to do after the shot
context: An ethical shot aims at the heart and lungs from a broadside or slightly quartering-away angle within the range you have practiced, so the animal goes down quickly. Also called where to shoot a deer, ethical shot, vital zone, heart lung shot, after the shot. Look for the animal standing still and broadside; a clear lane with no branches in the path.

title: Tracking a hit deer and reading a blood trail
context: Following a hit deer means starting at the spot it stood, finding hair and blood, and moving slowly from sign to sign while marking each spot. Also called blood trail, tracking a wounded deer, following blood, lost blood trail, how long to wait before tracking. Look for bright red, frothy blood often means a lung hit; dark blood or green matter can mean a gut hit and a longer wait.

title: When you cannot find the animal
context: When a hit animal cannot be found, the ethical next steps are a careful grid search, a second person's eyes, and, where the state allows it, a leashed tracking dog. Also called can't find my deer, lost the blood trail, wounded deer lost, deer ran off. Look for the last marked sign; water, thick cover, and downhill paths nearby.

title: Field dressing a deer
context: Field dressing a white-tailed or mule deer means removing the internal organs soon after the kill so body heat can escape and the meat can cool; wear gloves, tag the animal first if required, and keep the cavity clean. Also called gutting a deer, field dress, clean a deer, how to gut a deer, how do I field dress a deer. Look for gloves on, a sharp knife, and clean cloths or paper towels; a shallow belly cut with the blade edge up so the stomach and intestines are not opened.

title: Keeping game meat cool and spotting spoiled meat
context: Game meat stays safe when it is cooled below 40 °F (4 °C) quickly; in warm weather that means skinning, quartering, and icing within hours. Also called meat care warm weather, is my deer meat spoiled, hanging a deer, cooling venison, game meat spoiled. Look for air temperature above 40 °F means the clock is running; a sour or rotten smell, slime, or green color means spoiled.

title: Chronic wasting disease (CWD) and deer
context: Chronic wasting disease is a fatal prion disease of deer, elk, and moose; no human case has been confirmed, but health agencies advise people not to eat meat from an infected animal. Also called CWD, chronic wasting disease, zombie deer, sick looking deer, deer disease. Look for a thin, drooling, stumbling, or unafraid deer; animals found dead.

title: Cooking venison and wild game safely
context: Game meat is safest cooked to a measured temperature: rabbit and venison to 160 °F (71 °C), wild birds to 165 °F (74 °C), fish to 145 °F (63 °C), and bear or wild hog to at least 165 °F (74 °C) because of Trichinella. Also called venison temperature, cook deer meat, ground venison temperature, wild game cooking, venison cook temperature. Look for a food thermometer in the thickest part of the meat; ground meat and sausage cooked through, not judged by color.

title: Tree-stand safety
context: Tree-stand safety means staying attached to the tree from the moment you leave the ground until you are back on it, with a full-body harness and a lifeline or tether. Also called tree stand, deer stand fall, safety harness, full body harness, climbing a stand. Look for full-body harness worn and connected; stand straps and chains checked before each season.

title: Crossing fences and obstacles with a firearm
context: Crossing a fence, ditch, log, or stream with a firearm is safe only with the action open and the gun unloaded, set down on the far side with the muzzle pointed away. Also called crossing a fence with a gun, climbing over a log with a gun, crossing a stream with a rifle. Look for action open and chamber empty; muzzle pointed away from you and others.

title: Small game: rabbits, squirrels, and tularemia
context: Tularemia is a bacterial disease people can catch from handling or eating rabbits, hares, and rodents; gloves and thorough cooking prevent most cases. Also called rabbit fever, tularemia, cleaning rabbits, squirrel hunting safety. Look for a rabbit or squirrel that is slow, sick, or found dead; white spots on the liver. Wear gloves when skinning and cleaning, cook the meat thoroughly, and wash hands and tools afterward.

title: Waterfowl and migratory birds have their own rules
context: Ducks, geese, and other migratory birds are hunted under federal rules plus state rules, which differ from deer rules, including shot type and a federal duck stamp for many hunters. Also called duck hunting rules, goose hunting, migratory bird hunting, duck stamp, waterfowl regulations. Look for a federal duck stamp and state permits where required; non-toxic shot required for waterfowl.

title: Turkey hunting safety
context: Turkey hunting has its own risks because hunters wear camouflage and use calls, so another hunter can mistake a person for a bird. Also called turkey hunting, spring turkey safety, gobbler hunting, turkey call safety. Look for no red, white, or blue clothing, which can look like a gobbler's head; a tree trunk wider than your shoulders at your back.

title: Quartering and packing out game
context: Quartering means cutting a large animal into its four legs plus the backstraps, neck, and other meat so it can be carried out in loads and cooled faster; elk and moose often need this, and deer may too in warm weather. Also called quarter a deer, pack out meat, boning out a deer, how to quarter a deer. Look for clean game bags for each quarter and for the backstraps; a sharp knife, a spare blade, and a pack frame or sled for heavy loads.

title: Skinning and hanging a deer
context: Skinning removes the hide so meat can cool and stay clean; hanging lets the carcass cool and drain in cold, shaded, animal-proof conditions. Also called skin a deer, hang a deer, how long to hang venison, deer gambrel. Look for a stable gambrel or rope and a strong limb or beam; air at or below 40 °F (4 °C) for hanging. Hang by the hind legs or the head, skin from the top down with the blade edge out, and keep the carcass cold and covered from flies and animals.

title: Basic venison butchering cuts
context: Home butchering divides a deer into a few simple groups: backstraps and tenderloins for steaks, hind-quarter roasts, shoulder and neck for stew, and trim for grinding. Also called butcher a deer, venison cuts, backstrap, tenderloin, deer processing at home. Look for silver skin and fat trimmed off; a clean, cold work surface. Work cold and clean, trim fat, silver skin, and bloodshot meat, wrap tightly, label, and freeze.

title: Tagging, transport, and checking in game
context: Most states require you to tag an animal right away, keep the tag with it during transport, and report or check in the harvest within a set time. Also called tag a deer, check in deer, register harvest, transport deer legally. Look for the tag filled out and attached as your state requires; the state's online, phone, or station check-in. Read your state agency's current tagging and check-in page before the season and follow it exactly.

title: Using a processor when CWD is a concern
context: If you hunt where chronic wasting disease is found, ask a processor to process your animal by itself so its meat is not mixed with others. Also called deer processor CWD, individual processing, commercial processing venison. Look for the processor's policy on batch versus individual processing; test results before you eat the meat. Ask for individual processing, get the animal tested, and keep the meat frozen and unused until the result comes back.

title: Recovering game in water or thick cover
context: Getting an animal out of water, swamp, or thick cover comes after your own safety: cold water and deep mud can kill. Also called deer in the water, deer in a swamp, retrieve deer thick brush. Look for water depth, current, and temperature; ice that may not hold. Bring a partner and a rope, wait for light if needed, and reach the animal from shore or shallow water where you can.

title: Ground blind safety
context: A ground blind hides you at ground level, but it also hides you from other hunters, so safe setup matters. Also called ground blind, pop-up blind, hunting blind safety. Look for orange on the outside of the blind where required; a clear, safe shooting lane. Put orange on and around the blind as your state requires, know your shooting lanes and backstops, and keep the gun pointed out the window only when ready.

title: Hunting with a young or new hunter
context: Mentoring a new or young hunter means close supervision, short trips, and teaching safety before success. Also called take a kid hunting, mentor hunt, youth hunter, new hunter safety. Look for the new hunter within arm's reach when handling a gun; a completed hunter-education course where required. Keep sessions short and comfortable, review the firearm rules often, and check your state's youth and apprentice rules.

title: Black bear and moose around camps and carcasses
context: Black bears are drawn to carcasses, gut piles, and camp food, and a moose can charge if crowded, especially a cow with a calf or a bull in the rut. Also called bear at my deer, bear near camp, moose charge, bear safety hunting. Look for fresh bear sign near a gut pile or meat pole; a moose with ears back and hackles raised. Hang meat away from sleeping areas, store food sealed, approach a kill carefully and make noise, and give moose plenty of room.

title: Field dressing birds
context: Birds keep best when the crop and entrails are removed soon after the kill and the body is cooled. Also called clean a turkey, field dress a bird, gut a bird, dress a game bird. Look for gloves on; crop and intestines removed. Remove the entrails and crop, wipe the cavity, and cool the bird quickly; pluck or skin at home.

title: Lead versus non-lead ammunition
context: Lead bullets can break into small fragments in meat, and scavengers such as eagles can be poisoned by lead in gut piles; non-lead options exist. Also called lead bullet fragments, copper bullets, non-toxic shot, lead in venison. Look for fragments spread several inches from the wound channel; federal non-toxic shot rules for waterfowl. Trim generously around the wound channel, consider copper or other non-lead ammunition, and follow any rules where you hunt.

title: Hunting ethics: no waste, respect for land and people
context: Ethical hunting means taking only shots you can make cleanly, using the animal well, and respecting landowners, other hunters, and the law. Also called hunting ethics, fair chase, wanton waste, respect landowners. Look for permission in hand on private land; a plan to recover and use the meat. Practice before the season, pass on doubtful shots, recover and use what you take, and leave gates and land as you found them.

title: Land access, permission, and trespass
context: Hunting on private land needs the owner's permission, and posting and trespass rules differ from state to state; Yehsa has no property-owner map. Also called hunting private land, landowner permission, posted land, trespass hunting. Look for posted signs or paint marks on trees; a written or verbal permission you can show. Ask permission early, carry the owner's contact, learn your state's posting rules, and check official public-land maps.

title: Trapping is tightly regulated
context: Trapping usually needs its own license or education course and has strict rules on trap types, placement, checking times, and seasons. Also called trapping license, how to trap, trap rules, snare rules. Look for the state's trapper-education requirement; trap check intervals. Take your state's trapper-education course and follow its current rules.

title: Game cameras: etiquette and privacy
context: Trail cameras record whatever passes, including people, so place them where you have permission and think about privacy. Also called trail camera, game camera privacy, cellular trail cam. Look for the landowner's permission; trails used by hikers or neighbors. Get permission, aim cameras at game trails rather than paths people use, and check whether your state limits cellular cameras.

title: Wind direction and your scent
context: Deer rely on smell, and your scent drifts downwind in a widening cone, so hunters set up with the wind blowing from the deer toward them. Also called wind direction hunting, scent cone, deer smell me, play the wind. Look for wind direction from a light feather, milkweed fluff, or powder; thermals rising in the morning warmth and sinking in the evening.

title: Dragging a deer without hurting yourself
context: Dragging a deer is hard work that strains the back and heart, especially in cold weather and for people who do not exercise. Also called drag a deer, heart attack dragging deer, deer sled, moving a deer out. Look for chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness; a long or uphill drag. Use a sled or cart, get help, take frequent breaks, and quarter a large animal rather than drag it far.

title: Hunting alone: leave a plan
context: A solo hunter should leave a plan with someone: where you will park and sit, when you will be back, and when they should call for help. Also called solo hunting, hunting alone safety, tell someone where I hunt. Look for a marked map or pin of your stand; a check-in time. Leave the plan, carry a whistle, light, and first aid, and stick to your return time or update it.

title: Field dressing tools
context: A field dressing kit is a sharp knife and a spare blade, disposable gloves, clean cloths or paper towels, a tag, game bags, and a way to keep meat clean, dry, and cool. Also called field dressing kit, what do I need to field dress, game bags, dressing knife. Look for a sharp knife, a spare blade, and a small sharpener; disposable or rubber gloves, and eye protection for hogs and other high-risk game.

title: Field dressing an elk
context: Elk are large and hold heat, so the meat must be opened or quartered soon after the kill and cooled; many hunters use the gutless method to pack an elk out. Also called field dress an elk, how to field dress an elk, gut an elk, dress an elk, elk field dressing. Look for a carcass too heavy to drag far, with thick quarters and a lot of body heat; clean game bags, a sharp knife, gloves, and a pack frame for several loads.

title: Field dressing a moose
context: A moose is too large to cool as a whole carcass; the usual field care is to skin and quarter it, often with the gutless method, and hang the meat in clean game bags the same day. Also called field dress a moose, how to field dress a moose, gut a moose, dress a moose, moose field dressing. Look for a very large, heavily muscled carcass that stays warm inside for hours; several game bags, gloves, a sharp knife, a saw or axe, rope, and a way to pack heavy loads.

title: Field dressing a pronghorn
context: A pronghorn is a small, thin-skinned plains animal that spoils quickly in heat, so it should be field dressed or skinned soon after the kill, kept free of hair, and cooled the same day. Also called field dress a pronghorn, field dress an antelope, gut a pronghorn, pronghorn field care, clean a pronghorn. Look for a slim carcass and a thin hide whose hair slips and sticks to meat easily; warm, open country with little shade.

title: Field dressing a black bear
context: Black bear meat must be handled with gloves, cooled after the thick fat is dealt with, and cooked to a measured 165 °F (74 °C) because bears can carry Trichinella; freezing does not reliably kill it. Also called field dress a bear, field dress a black bear, gut a bear, bear trichinella, cook bear meat. Look for a thick hide and a heavy fat layer that holds heat in the carcass; gloves on, and a clean knife kept off the gut contents.

title: Field dressing a wild hog
context: Wild hogs, or feral swine, can carry brucellosis and Trichinella, so you should wear gloves and eye protection while dressing them, keep bare skin off fluids and organs, and cook the meat thoroughly. Also called field dress a hog, field dress a wild boar, gut a hog, feral hog brucellosis, clean a wild hog. Look for a bristly hog with a thick hide and, often, sharp tusks; gloves and eye protection on before you open the carcass.

title: Cleaning a rabbit or hare
context: Cleaning a rabbit or hare means skinning and gutting it with gloves on, checking the liver, cooling the meat, and cooking it to 160 °F (71 °C), because rabbits and hares can carry tularemia. Also called clean a rabbit, gut a rabbit, field dress a rabbit, clean a hare, how to clean a rabbit. Look for gloves on before you skin or gut the animal; a liver without white spots; white spots are a warning.

title: Cleaning a squirrel
context: Cleaning a squirrel means skinning and gutting it with gloves on, cooling the meat, and cooking it thoroughly, because squirrels and other rodents can carry tularemia. Also called clean a squirrel, gut a squirrel, field dress a squirrel, how to clean a squirrel. Look for gloves on before you skin or gut the squirrel; a liver without white spots.

title: Field dressing a turkey
context: Field dressing a turkey means removing the entrails and the crop soon after the kill, cooling the bird, and later cooking all turkey meat to 165 °F (74 °C). Also called gut a turkey, field dress a turkey, how to gut a turkey, dress a turkey. Look for gloves on, and a way to open the body cavity without bursting the gut or the crop; the crop emptied or removed at the base of the neck.

title: Field dressing grouse, pheasant, and quail
context: Upland birds such as grouse, pheasant, and quail keep best when the crop and entrails come out soon after the kill and the birds are cooled, then cooked to 165 °F (74 °C). Also called gut a pheasant, field dress grouse, clean a quail, field dress a pheasant, gut a grouse. Look for gloves on, and entrails and crop removed while the bird is still fresh; birds kept separate, cool, and dry, not in a warm pile.

title: Field dressing ducks and geese
context: Ducks and geese should be gutted and cooled soon after the kill, cooked to 165 °F (74 °C), and transported with the head or one fully feathered wing still attached until you are home, unless a stated exception applies. Also called dress a duck, field dress a duck, gut a goose, clean a duck, field dress a goose. Look for gloves on, entrails removed, and the bird kept cool and dry; the head or one fully feathered wing still on the bird during transport from the field.

title: Gutless method
context: The gutless method is a way to skin and quarter a large animal, such as an elk or a moose, without first removing the guts, so the meat can be packed out in loads and cooled the same day. Also called gutless quartering, quarter an elk, quarter a moose, bone out an elk, gutless field dressing. Look for the animal on its side, one half of the hide skinned back as a clean work surface; front and hind quarters, backstraps, and tenderloins going into clean, dry game bags.

title: Evidence of sex, tagging, and the waterfowl wing rule
context: Many hunts require you to tag the animal promptly and leave evidence of sex naturally attached to the meat, and federal migratory-bird rules require the head or one fully feathered wing to stay on most waterfowl during transport. Also called evidence of sex, leave proof of sex, fully feathered wing, tagging and evidence of sex, proof of sex on a quarter.

title: Disease signs while dressing game
context: While you dress game, look at the animal and its organs for signs of disease: a thin, stumbling, or unafraid deer, an animal found dead, or a liver with white spots, and do not eat a suspect animal. Also called white spots on the liver, liver spots on game, sick looking game, inspect the liver, spots on a deer liver.

title: Deer scat
context: Deer scat is a pile of small, dark, oval or acorn-shaped pellets, often 20 to 50 together, that shows where deer have fed or bedded. Also called deer droppings, deer poop, deer pellets, deer poo, deer dung. Look for pellets about 1/2 to 3/4 inch (1.5 to 2 cm) long, often with a small point or dimple at one end; dark and shiny when fresh, dull and dry or crumbly when old.

title: Deer tracks
context: A deer track is a split, heart-shaped hoof print made by two pointed toes, about 2 to 3 1/2 inches (5 to 9 cm) long. Also called deer track, deer prints, deer hoof print, whitetail track, deer sign. Look for two teardrop toes forming a heart with the point toward travel; two dewclaw dots behind the print in mud, snow, or when running.

title: Deer rubs
context: A rub is a sapling or small tree where a buck has scraped off bark with his antlers, mostly in fall before and during the rut. Also called buck rub, antler rub, rubs on trees, scraped bark, deer sign. Look for bark stripped from one side of a small tree, often 1 to 4 inches (2.5 to 10 cm) thick, from knee to waist height; pale fresh wood, shredded bark curls on the ground, and broken twigs.

title: Deer scrapes
context: A scrape is a patch of bare earth that a buck paws clear under an overhanging branch and marks with scent, mostly in the weeks before the rut. Also called buck scrape, deer scrape, scrape under a branch, licking branch, deer sign. Look for a pawed oval of bare dirt, often 1 to 3 feet (30 to 90 cm) across; a chewed or broken licking branch about head height above it.

title: Reading deer sign
context: Deer sign is the tracks, scat, rubs, scrapes, beds, and browsed plants that deer leave, and reading it shows where they travel, feed, and rest. Also called deer sign, signs of deer, how to scout for deer, deer scouting, where are the deer. Look for trails and tracks between thick cover and food; scat piles, oval beds pressed in leaves or snow.
